questions.question: Design a chat/messaging system like WhatsApp that supports one-on-one and group messaging.
questions.title: Design a Chat/Messaging System (WhatsApp)
questions.direct_answer: Use WebSocket connections for real-time message delivery with a message queue (Kafka) for reliability. Store messages in Cassandra partitioned by conversation ID. Maintain a presence service in Redis for online/offline status. Fan-out on write for small groups, fan-out on read for large broadcast channels.

interviewer_intent.testing: Real-time messaging architecture, WebSocket management, message ordering and delivery guarantees, storage partitioning
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Polling HTTP for new messages instead of persistent connections — adds seconds of latency and wastes server resources at scale
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss message ordering with vector clocks or server-assigned sequence numbers, end-to-end encryption trade-offs, and graceful offline message queuing with delivery receipts

sections.title: Why HTTP Polling Is a Non-Starter at Messaging Scale
sections.content:
A WhatsApp-scale system handles **2 billion registered users**, roughly **100 million daily active**, each sending ~40 messages per day. That is **4 billion messages daily ÷ 86,400 seconds ≈ 46,000 messages/second** average, with peaks at 3–5× during evening hours — **~200K msg/sec**. The real bottleneck is not message throughput but **connection count**: 100 million concurrent WebSocket connections across a fleet of gateway servers.

The most common design mistake is using **HTTP polling** — clients repeatedly ask "any new messages?" every few seconds. With 100M users polling every 5 seconds, that is **20 million requests/second**, of which 95% return nothing. This wastes server capacity and adds 2–5 seconds of artificial latency to every message. Persistent **WebSocket connections** solve both problems: the server pushes messages the instant they arrive, delivering sub-300ms latency.

Storage requirements compound the challenge: 4B messages/day × 500 bytes average = **2TB/day** of message data. With 1-year retention, that is **730TB** — ruling out any single-node relational database. Messages are write-heavy and read-sequentially (chat history scrollback), pointing to **Cassandra** or a similar LSM-tree store optimized for append-heavy workloads with partition-key locality.

sections.title: WebSocket Gateways and the Session Registry Pattern
sections.content:
Each client opens a **persistent WebSocket connection** to a gateway server. Modern gateway servers using epoll-based I/O can hold **500K–1M idle connections** on a single machine (32GB RAM, Linux kernel tuned with increased file descriptor limits). For 100M concurrent users, the system needs **100–200 gateway instances** behind a load balancer.

When a client connects, the gateway registers a session mapping in **Redis**: `session:{userId} → {gatewayId}`. When User A sends a message to User B, the message service looks up B's gateway in Redis — an O(1) operation — and forwards the message to that specific gateway, which pushes it down B's WebSocket. If User B has no Redis entry (offline), the message is persisted to the durable store and a **push notification** (FCM for Android, APNs for iOS) fires to wake the device.

The architecture keeps routing stateless even though connections are stateful.

```
Client A ──WebSocket──→ Gateway-3
                           │
                     ┌─────┴──────┐
                     │  Message   │
                     │  Service   │
                     └─────┬──────┘
                           │ lookup user B → Redis → gateway-7
                           │
                     Gateway-7 ──WebSocket──→ Client B
                           │
                     If offline → Cassandra + Push Notification
```

Gateway servers are **stateful** (they hold connections), but the message routing service is **stateless** — any instance can route any message by querying Redis. This separation matters for operations: you can roll gateway servers with connection draining while message services deploy independently and instantly.

sections.title: Cassandra for Message Storage: Partitioned by Conversation
sections.content:
Messages need a storage engine that excels at **high write throughput** and sequential reads (chat history scrollback). **Cassandra** fits naturally: its LSM-tree architecture is optimized for append-heavy workloads, and leaderless replication with tunable consistency gives multi-datacenter availability without complex shard management.

The schema places all messages for one conversation in a single partition, ordered chronologically by a time-ordered UUID.

```sql
CREATE TABLE messages (
    conversation_id  UUID,
    message_id       TIMEUUID,
    sender_id        UUID,
    content          TEXT,
    content_type     TEXT,
    media_url        TEXT,
    status           TEXT,
    created_at       TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);
```

Reading the last 50 messages is a single partition read with `LIMIT 50` — the most efficient query Cassandra can execute. Write consistency uses `LOCAL_QUORUM` (2 of 3 replicas in the local datacenter acknowledge) while reads use `LOCAL_ONE` for lower latency, since chat history tolerates brief staleness.

**Why not PostgreSQL?** At 46K writes/second average with 200K peaks, a single Postgres instance would need aggressive sharding from day one. Cassandra's built-in partitioning eliminates shard management overhead, and its leaderless design avoids single-writer bottlenecks. Each conversation's messages are co-located on the same partition, so scrollback reads never span multiple nodes.

sections.title: Message Ordering: Sequence Numbers Beat Vector Clocks
Group Messaging: When Fan-Out on Write Becomes Expensive
Failure Modes: What Breaks and How the System Self-Heals
sections.content:
**Gateway crash** — the user's WebSocket drops. The client reconnects (with exponential backoff and jitter) to any available gateway, re-registers in Redis, and pulls missed messages by sequence number. Messages queued during disconnection are durable in Cassandra, so nothing is lost.

**Redis (session registry) down** — gateways can't route messages to specific peers. The fallback is **topic-based broadcasting**: publish the message to a Kafka topic partitioned by user ID, and let each gateway consume messages for its connected users. Slower but functional. Redis Sentinel or Cluster provides HA to minimize this scenario's duration.

**Cassandra node failure** — replication factor 3 means losing one node has zero impact on reads or writes at `LOCAL_QUORUM`. Cassandra's hinted handoff and repair handle node recovery automatically with no operator intervention.

**Thundering herd on reconnection** — after a major outage, millions of clients reconnect simultaneously. Rate-limit reconnection with **jittered backoff** on the client side, and use connection admission control on gateways (reject with `Retry-After` header if at capacity). Without this, the reconnection storm can crash the gateways that just recovered.

**Message ordering violation** — network reordering can cause messages to arrive out of sequence. The per-conversation sequence number lets clients reorder locally. If a gap persists beyond 5 seconds, the client fetches missing messages from the REST API as a self-healing fallback.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **WebSocket + Redis session map for O(1) routing** — persistent connections deliver sub-300ms latency.
- **Cassandra partitioned by conversation_id** — LSM-tree architecture handles append-heavy message writes.
- **Server-assigned sequence numbers per conversation** — Redis INCR gives monotonically increasing IDs per conversation.
- **Fan-out on write for groups <100; fan-out on read for larger** — small groups copy message references to each member inbox (fast reads).
- **Offline message queue with 30-day retention** — Kafka topic per user for undelivered messages; consumer is the gateway.
- **End-to-end encryption: Signal Protocol** — X3DH key agreement on session establishment; Double Ratchet for forward secrecy.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A WhatsApp-scale chat system handles 100 million daily active users generating roughly 46,000 messages per second average, peaking at 200,000 during evening hours. The most important design decision is transport — HTTP polling disqualifies itself immediately because it requires 95% of requests to return empty responses and adds seconds of latency.

**The WebSocket gateway and routing:**
- Each client opens a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server; modern Linux servers with epoll-based I/O can hold 500K–1M idle connections with tuned file descriptor limits; 100M concurrent users needs 100–200 gateway instances
- When a client connects, the gateway registers a session mapping in Redis: `userId → gatewayId`; when User A sends to User B, the message service does an O(1) Redis lookup and forwards directly to B's gateway without broadcasting to all gateways
- Message delivery latency is consistently sub-300ms end-to-end with this architecture

**Storage — Cassandra for the message log:**
- Cassandra's LSM-tree architecture handles append-heavy write workloads; partition by conversation_id so all messages for one chat are co-located; cluster by TIMEUUID for chronological ordering
- 4 billion messages/day at ~1KB each = 4TB/day; with replication factor 3, that's 12TB/day of total storage; Cassandra scales horizontally by adding nodes, each absorbing 1/N of the new data

**The hard problems:**
- Message ordering: the server assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number per conversation using Redis INCR; clients detect gaps and request missing messages; simpler and sufficient compared to vector clocks
- Group fan-out: groups under 100 members use fan-out-on-write (pre-deliver to each member inbox); larger groups and broadcast channels use fan-out-on-read (store once, deliver on access) to avoid 10,000-write amplification per message
- Offline delivery: messages are retained in Cassandra; reconnecting clients replay from their last acknowledged sequence number

I recommend WebSocket gateways with Redis session routing, Cassandra for message storage, server-assigned sequence numbers for ordering, and the hybrid fan-out strategy with a configurable threshold between write and read fan-out.
